Financial package for sick SSIs 
*122. PROF. MM. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have proposed to give any financial 
package for revival of sick small scale industries in the country; 
(b) if so, the amount allocated for this purpose by Government during the 
current year; and 
(c) the funds released by Government so far? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRIMAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) to (c) A statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Central Government does not provide any financial assistance 
for rehabilitation of sick Small Scale Industries (SSIs). 
However, financial assistance, by way of debt restructuring, including fresh 
loans, etc., for the rehabilitation of sick SSI is provided by the primary lending 
institutions (PLI), including the commercial banks. For this purpose, the 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued guidelines to banks from time to time 
on detection of sickness in SSI at an early stage and taking remedial measures 
and for rehabilitation of sick SSI units identified as potentially viable. 
After the detailed guidelines of January 2002, the RBI has issued 
fresh guidelines on 8th September 2005, based on the "Policy Package" 
for Stepping up Credit to Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) 
announced by the Central Government on 10th August, 2005. These 
guidelines related, inter alia, to viability criteria, prudential norms for 
restructured accounts, provision of additional finance, time frame for 
working out the restructuring package and its implementation, etc.  
The banks have also been advised by the RBI to review the progress in 
rehabilitation and restructuring of SME accounts on a quarterly basis. The State 
Level Inter-Institutional Committee (SLIIC), set up in each State

under the convenorship of the RBI representative, has also been advised to 
monitor, inter alia, the implementation of these guidelines. 
(b) and (c) In view of the foregoing, do not arise.

Statement 
(a) and (b) The lawyers under the banner of Delhi Bar Association have been on 
strike from 2nd January, 2006 in protest against the shifting of some courts from Tis Hazari 
to the new Court Complex at Rohini. A section of lawyers have been obstructing the 
working of Tis Hazari and Rohini Courts. 
(c) The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi vide its resolution dated 10.01.2006 has, 
inter-alia, resolved that the District Judge shall arrange for adequate police force to be 
kept in reserve in the judgeship, to be deployed for protection of judicial officers, 
lawyers, litigants, court staff and the court property, and if possible video cameras 
should also be used. The resolution further says that the district judge should inform 
names of the persons involved in disrupting the court proceedings to the High Court 
forthwith so that appropriate proceedings for contempt of court can be taken. However, if 
any law and order problem arises, necessary action w ill be taken by the 
Government as per law.

confrontation between the bench and the bar in Delhi Tis Hazari Courts; 
42

modalities whereby off-repeated strikes by lawyers paralyzing the working of the 
Courts could be eliminated; and

that video cameras be used to identify troublemakers and if need be, police can 
be called and contempt action initiated in view of the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) As per Article 227 of the Constitution of India, the power of 
superintendence on all Courts and Tribunals lies with the Hon'ble High Courts. 
Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in ex. Captain Harish Uppal Vs Union of 
India (2003) 2SCC 45 and in various others cases has held that the advocates 
have no right to go on strike. It may also be added that as per Section 6 (1) (c)

cases of misconduct against advocates on its roll. The Hon'ble High Court of 
Delhi vide its resolution dated 10.01.2006 has, inter-alia, resolved that the 
District Judge shall arrange for adequate police force to be kept in reserve in 
the judgeship, to be deployed for protection of judicial officers, lawyers, 
litigants, court staff and the court pr operty, and if possible video cameras 
should also be used. The resolution further says that the district judge should 
infrom the names of the persons involved in disrupting the court proceedings to 
the High Court forthwith so that appropriate proceedings for contempt of court can 
be taken. However, if any law and other problem arises, necessary action will 
be taken by the Government as per law.

† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

cut-off from the rest of the world for six months and the telecommunication 
facilities also come to a standstill due to lack of sufficient staff; and

providing appropriate telecom service in those areas in winters? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICA-
TIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD):

telecommunication systems/augmentation of existing systems are taken up as 
regular activity for further improvement of telecom facilities.

(a) No, Sir, Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF) is supporting the

Objectives of setting up of IIMs 
753. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA:  Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the objectives and original intent in setting up the Indian 
Institutes of Management at various cities; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the IIMs are largely catering to MNCs; 
(c) the steps to be taken by Government to review the utility of these 
institutions; and 
(d) the steps proposed to chan ge the goals, objectives and 
orientations of IIMs in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to 
(d) Broadly the Indian Institute of Ma nagement (IIMs) were set up with the 
objectives of imparting high quality management education and training, 
conducting research and providing consul tancy services in the field of 
management to various sectors of the Indian economy. These are the premier 
educational institutions catering to the development of the nation's managerial 
manpower. Various placement agencies both from private as well as public 
sector visit these institutes every year to select the candidates from amongst 
the MM students to meet their requir ements. IIMs do not encourage their 
students to take up any particular type of work. The students are free to take 
up a job of their choice. The alumni of the IIMs have distinguished 
themselves in all sectors, not just with MNCs. To meet the demand, the 
Government has suggested the IIMs to create more opportunities for students in 
the country by increasing intake capacity, creation of additional infrastructure 
and introduction of new courses. Over the years the IIMs have developed their 
own brand image and there is no question of changing the goals, objectives 
and orientation of these Institutes.

Under the Scheme of Deen Dayal Disabled Rehabilitation implemented by the 
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment, establishment of special schools is 
encouraged by providing grant in aid to the public institutions and voluntary 
organisations for imparting special education to the mentally challenged, hearing 
and speech impaired, visually challenged, etc., free of cost. The special schools

objective of brining about varying degrees of improvement in the lives of the 
children with disabilities. More than 350 schools and 140 vocational training

following activities: 
- Early detection and identification. 
- Provisions of aids and appliances. 
- Teacher Training. 
- Resource support. 
- Community awareness and parental counselling.

767. SHRI R.K. ANAND^Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE

girl education had recommended 50 per cent reservation at the entry level for girls in 
regular schools; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the incentives provided to encourage girls education? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) A 
committee of Central Advisory Board of Education on Girls Education and Common School 
System in its report submitted in June, 2005 has recommended that "girls students should

programme or alternative systems in a multi-track approach. Girls deserve to have upto 
108

50% of the seats reserved for them at the entry points of the regular schools". 
(c) Some of the incentives provided under "Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan" to encourage 
girls' education at elementary level are as follows:— 
(i) Free textbooks for girls upto class VIII within the ceiling limit of Rs. 150 
per child. 
(ii) Separate toilets for girls. 
(iii) At least 50% of the teachers to be appointed should be women. 
(iv) The National Programme for Education of Girls at the Elementary Level 
(NPEGEL) provides for development of a "model school" in every cluster 
with intensive community mobilization and supervision of girls enrolment 
in schools. Gender sensitization of teachers, development of gender-sensitive 
learning materials, and provision of need based incentives like escorts, 
stationery, work books and uniforms are some of the endeavours under the 
programme. 
(v) Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV), a new scheme for setting up 
of residential schools with boarding facilities at elementary level. 
Some of the incentives provided by the Central Government at secondary 
level are as under:— 
(i) All girl students who are single children of their parents appearing in the merit 
list of All India Pre-Medical Test (AIPMT) and All India Engineering 
Entrance Examination (AIEEE) and pursuing medical/engineering courses in 
institutes participating in AIPMT/ AIEEE or in the Central Government 
controlled or aided institutions will be eligible for scholarship. 
(ii) Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan provides hostel facility for girls. 
(iii) 33% of the seats in Navodaya Vidyalayas are reserved for girls.

of boarding and hostel facilities for girls.

autonomous body set up under the Press Council Act 1978, with the twin objective

standards of newspapers and news agencies in India and to inculcate principles 
of self regulation among the press. The Government follows a policy of non-
interference in the functioning of the Council and it enjoys complete 
autonomy in its functioning. The Council, which is in a nature of a self 
regulatory body of the Press, has built "Norms of Journalistic Conduct", which 
cover the principles and ethics with regard to Journalism, as also guidelines

provisions of the Norms of Journalistic Conduct Concerning Advertisements 
36(H) - No advertisements shall be published which promotes directly or

wine, alcohol, liquor and other intoxicants. The advisories issued by the Press 
Council of India, however, carry only mo ral force and are not enforceable in

Streamlining of judicial system 
† 812. PROF.ALKABALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have carried out any extensive study with regard to 
Judicial Administration Penal Code and present system of legal proceedings; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) Government's and Judiciary's reaction thereto; 
(d) whether Government have any proposal to give a new form to Judiciary to 
streamline it and make it accessible for common man in order to make it popular; 
and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
148 

[27 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND 
JUSTICE (SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) and (b) Government had set up 
a Committee, under the Chairmanship of Justice V.S. Malimath, former Chief 
Justice of Ksrnataka High Court and Kerala High Court, on the reforms in 
Criminal Justice System. The Committee submitted its report in April, 2003 
and had given several recommendations relating to Criminal Justice System. 
The Committee also gave recommendations on raising the working days of 
the Supreme Court and High Courts, preparing an arrear eradication scheme, 
summary disposal of cases, imparting sp ecialized training to judges, better 
facilities for witnesses etc. 
(c) These recommendations were forw arded to all the Registrars 
General of Supreme Court and High Courts. 
(d) and (e) Government has taken seve ral measures to streamline the 
judicial system. In order to make justice accessible to common man special 
tribunals and courts like Central Ad ministrative Tribunal, Family Courts, 
Labour Courts have been set up. The Government has also computerised 
Metropolitan city courts and capital city courts so that l itigants can access the 
cause-list, daily orders and judgements through the Internet. The project for 
computerization of all the Subordinate Courts in the country has also been 
finalized for implementation.

813. SHRI R.K. ANAND: Will th e Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) what was the allocation for judiciary in the Ninth and Tenth Five Year 
Plans; 
(b) whether it is a fact that to clear all pending cases in the courts, 
manifold increase in the number of judg es is needed which is in turn would 
need increase in infrastructure and support staff while allocation to judiciary 
in the Ninth and Tenth Five Year Plans is approximately 0.07 per cent; and 
(c) whether it is also a fact that as the subordinate courts lack basic 
amenities, diversion of funds would further deteriorate the working 
environment? 
149 

RAJYASABHA [27 February, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE 
(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) The allocation for judiciary in the Ninth and Tenth 
Five Year Plan was Rs. 384.00 crore and Rs. 700 crore respectively. 
(b) and (c) Judge strength for High Courts is reviewed every three years by 
Department of Justice. The next review is being undertaken during 2006. Judge 
strength for the Subordinate judiciary is reviewed by the concerned State 
Governments. The expenditure in respect of High Courts and Subordinate 
Courts (including the provision for infrastructural facilities) is to be met by the 
concerned State Governments. The Centrally Sponsored Scheme for development of 
infrastructure facilities for the judiciary is being implemented only to augment the 
resources of the State Governments.

Objectives of the National Judicial Academy:— 
(i) to provide training to the J udicial Officers of the States/Union 
Territories; 
(ii) to provide facilities for training of the ministerial officers working in 
the Supreme Court of India; 
(iii) to study the Court Management and Administration of Justice in the 
States/Union Territories and to suggest improvements to the said 
system; 
(iv) to prescribe rules and regulations for the management and 
administration of the Society; 
(v) to undertake, organize and fac ilitate study courses, conferences, 
seminars and lectures and research in matters relating to Court 
Management and Administration of Justice; 
(vi) to establish the Society as  a centre of excellence in Court 
Management; 
162 

[27 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(vii) to provide and disseminate information and literature relating to 
judicial administration; 
(viii) to conduct or sponsor training programmes for judicial officers and 
court administrators dealing with aspects of court and case flow 
management and court technology (computers); 
(ix) to provide continuing judicial education to judicial officers of the 
States/Union Territories; 
(x) to assist and promote education and skills programmes aimed at to 
promote the highest standard of professional competence and 
practice; 
(xi) to establish Regional Centres at convenient locations in India to 
promote the objects of the Society; 
(xii) to establish liaison with resear ch institutions, universities and other 
bodies for the purpose of helping the cause of administration of 
Justice; 
(xiii) to enhance the capabilities of the existing training institutions for 
Judicial Officers of the States/U nion Territories, to improve their 
quality of training; 
(xiv) to assist, interact and collaborate in promoting study of court 
management with other institutions and bodies, both within the 
country and abroad; 
(xv) to undertake publication of papers, books, monographs, journals etc. in 
Court Management and Administration of Justice; 
(xvi) to publish and disseminate information relating to results of research 
and other training courses/programmes; 
(xvii) to award certificates and othe r distinctions to Judicial Officers 
trained and to prescribe standards of proficiency before awarding of 
such certificates and other distinctions; 
(xviii) to establish procedures for smooth functioning of the Society and 
carry out activities in matters re lating to personnel, finances, 
administration, purchases and management of hostels etc.; 
(xix) to do all such other lawful acts and things as are conductive or 
incidental to the attainment of the objectives of the Society. 
 
Delimitation of constituencies 
 
816. SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Will the Minister of LAW 
AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2006] 
(a) whether the process of delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly 
constituencies has been completed by the Delimitation Commission; 
(b) if not, the States and Union Territories in which the process has not been 
completed; 
(c) the States and Union Territories where the process is on; 
(d) the States and Union Territories where the process has not commenced

(e) by when the new proposals will come into force;

process has been completed; and

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) to

817. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in the event of strike by lawyers, the litigants can 
henceforth plead their own cases and cross examine the witnesses-in criminal trials 
in Courts; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the reaction of Bar Associations thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ):  
(a) to (b) On 10.01.2006, the full court of the High Court of Delhi passed  
164 

[27 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
a resolution in the following terms:— 
"A Section of lawyers at Tis Hazari Court, Delhi, have been on strike from 
02.01.2006 against the creation of the Rohini Court, Delhi. On 04.01.2006 these lawyers 
went to the Supreme Court of India and shouted abusive slogans against Hon'ble the Chief 
Justice of India, Hon'ble the Chief Justice, Delhi High Court, and others. On 
06.01.2006 at the inauguration of the Rohini Court, they again went to Rohini and 
shouted abusive slogans and created nuisance. Thereafter they have been obstructing 
the working of the Tis Hazari and Rohini Court. 
These lawyers have been committing violence and agitations as is evident from the 
reports received from the Distt. Judge, Tis Hazari and Judge-ln-Charge, Rohini Court, 
Delhi. They have been beating other lawyers who wanted to work, and catching them 
by collars and pulling them out of the court when these lawyers wanted to enter the court 
rooms, to argue their cases. 
Earlier the striking lawyers declared that they will strike up to 10.01.06 and hence this 
court was maintaining restraint and it also asked the police to maintain restraint as the High 
Court did not want to aggravate the situation. 
On 09.01.2006, report came from the Distt., Judge, Tis Hazari Court, that a Resolution 
has been passed that the Strike would continue up to 18.01.06 and there is no certainty 
that the strike will not continue even thereafter. This strike is causing great hardship to the 
litigant public whose urgent applications, such as bail, injunction applications, cannot be 
heard because of the strike. Litigants/witnesses etc. come from distant places at heavy 
expenses, who are being told that their cases cannot be taken up due to the strike. This is 
most unfair to the litigant public. 
This is a sovereign institution and we will maintain our authority at all costs. No 
one can be allowed to hold the judiciary at ransom. The Court cannot standby and see 
the institution paralized indefinitely. 
The Court has exercised great restraint from 02.01.2006 till today and had thought 
that the strike of Tis Hazari lawyers will be over today, i.e. 10.01.2006, but now it appears 
that there is a section of the Tis Hazari lawyers who are determined to continue the strike 
indefinitely. This state of affairs cannot be tolerated any longer. The lawyers must know 
that enough and everything has a limit. 
The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the lawyer's strike are illegal and that 
effective steps should be taken to stop the growing 
165 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2006] 
tendency. In Paadurang Duttaram Khadekar Vs. Bar Council of Maharashtra 
(1284) 2 SCC 556, Tahil Ram Issar Oas Sadarangam Vs. Ramchand Issuradas 
Sadarangam 1993(3) SSC 256, Common Clause A Registered Society Vs. Union of India 
(1996) 3 SSC 19, Sajeev Dutta Vs. Ministry of Information & Broadcasting (1995) 3 
SSC 619, Indian Council of Legal & Advice Vs. Bar Council of India 1995(1) SSC 732, 
K. John Koshi Vs. Dr. Tarai Eshwar Prasad Shaw (1998) 8 SCC 024; Mahabir Prasad Singh Vs. 
Jacks Aviation (P) Ltd. 1999(1) SCC 37 and Ex. Captain Harish Uppal Vs. Union of India 
(2003) 2 SSC 45, it was held by the Supreme Court that the advocates have no right to 
go on strike. The Courts are under no obligation to adjourn matters because lawyers are 
on strike. On the contrary, it is the duty of ail courts to go on with matters on their boards 
even in the absence of lawyers. In other words, courts must not be privy to strikes or 
calls for boycotts. It was held that if a lawyer, holding a vakalatnama of a client, 
abstains from attending court due to a strike calf, he shall be personally liable to pay costs, 
which shall be in addition to damages which he might have to pay to his client for the loss 
suffered by him. In spite of repeated pronouncements by the Supreme Court, the Lawyers' 
strikes have continued unabated. 
The judiciary is accountable to the pubiic. The dispensation of justice must not stop 
for any reason. The strike by lawyers have iawered the image of the judiciary in the 
eyes of the general public. 
The Supreme Court held that right to speedy justice is included in Article 21 of 
the Constitution of India. In A.R.'Antulay Vs. R.S. Nayak (1992) 1 SSC 225 and Rai 
Deo Sharma Vs. State of Bihar (1998) 7 SCC 507; it was held that the litigant has a right to 
speedy justice. The lawyers' strikes, however, are denying these rights to the citizens in 
the State. 
In Manpj Kumar Vs. Civil Judge, Deoria (Writ Petition No. 33778 of 1997 decided 
on 10.10.1997) a Division Bench of the Ailahabad High Court observed; "Before 
parting with this case, we would like to mention that it is deeply regrettable and highly 
objectionable that there are strikes in District Courts in U.P. on flimsy and frivolous pretext, 
and some, district Courts function only for about 60 or 70 days in a year. This is a shocking 
state of affairs, and will no longer be tolerated by this court. The judiciary and bar are both 
accountable to the public and they must behave in a responsible manner so that cases are 
decided quickly and thus the faith of the public in the judiciary is maintained. Surely, the 
public has a right to expect this from us. We therefore, issue a general mandamus to all the 
judicial officers in all Distt. Courts in U.P. that if the lawyers go on strike 
166 

[27 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
the judicial officers must, despite the st rike of lawyers, sit in court and pass 
orders in cases before them even in the absence of the counsels. If the lawyers 
disturb the functioning of the Court, the District Judge shall contact the police 
and the police will give all protection to the judges and the cases w ill not be 
adjourned merely because of the lawyers'  strike. People in this State are fed 
up with lawyers' strikes and this state of affairs must now end. The lawyers 
must realize that litigants, witnesses, etc. often come from distant places at 
heavy expense and it is most improper th at they have to go away because of 
strikes by lawyers." 
In M/s. Suresh Chandra Varshney & Co. Vs. State of U.P. (Writ 
Petition No. 15342 of 2000 decided on 30.03.2000), this court observed that "It 
has come to our notice that in about half of the District Courts in the State of 
U.P. the lawyers are on strike for about a month and they are no permitting any 
judicial authority to work. This is deeply regrettable and highly objectionable. 
The judiciary exists for the people and not for the lawyers and judges. In our 
view the attitude of the lawyers of the District courts and Commissioners of 
U.P. who are on strike for the last about one month is most irresponsible. This 
act of the iawyers will no longer be tolerated by this Court and nobody will be 
allowed to hold the judiciary to ransom. A Division Bench of this Court of 
Manoj Kumar Vs. Civil Judge, 1997(3) UPLEEC 1767 has held that if lawyers 
go on strike even then courts must sit and pass judicial orders even in absence 
of the lawyers and if the functioning of the court is disturbed by anybody 
police help must be taken by the Distt. Judge or other Presiding Officer. The 
people of the State are fed up with lawyers' Strike and they are suffering greatly. 
The lawyers must understand that litigants, witness etc. Come to Court from 
far off places often at heavy expenses but they find that the courts are closed 
just because the lawyers are on stri ke. This is most unfair to the litigants or 
their witnesses. We, therefore, direct the Judges of all District Courts, 
Commissioners, and other Presiding Officers of the Courts or authorities, whether 
judicial or quasi judicial , hearing the cases and pass orders even in the 
absence of the lawyers who are on strike. If anybody disturbs the working of 
the courts the District Judge, Collector, Commissioner or the Presiding Officer of 
the Court or Tribunal or authority shall call the police and prevent them from 
doing so. The lawyers must know that enough is enough". 
in Siddhartha Kumar Vs. Upper Civil Judge, Ghazipur (1998) 1 
UPLBEC 587 the Division Bench observed 'Nothing more is required to be 
added on this score except that those Presiding Officers (though their 
167 

RAJYASABHA [27 February, 2006] 
number is very little) who have developed vested interest in the strikes to be dealt with 
sternly. They became party to engineer a strike on particular days. One of us (Justice O.P. 
Garg), on the basis of long standing experience of the working of the District Courts, 
may venture to say that some Presiding Officer become restive if for a long spell of time 
there is no strike. Feelers are sent to the members of the Bar to go on strike so that the 
monotony and drudgery be broken to have a respite. The period of strike is not meant for 
rejoining, jubilation or merry-making. Hereafter, the Presiding Officers shall not be granted 
any remission in their out-turn of work due to the strike by the lawyers. The period of 
strike days shall also be computed towards working days and the out-turn of work shall 
be calculated with reference...". 
No one has a right to obstruct the administration of justice. An extraordinary 
situation demands extraordinary measures to be taken. Where the fundamental rights of 
the citizens are being grossly violated, the High Court as a guardian of Subordinate Courts 
and as a protector of 'rights of the citizens' would not sit quiet and allow the situation 
to deteriorate, it is absolutely necessary that very strong measures should be taken to stop 
the growing tendency of lawyers' strikes. The Courts now feel that the time has come to 
take immediate effective and strong steps, to remedy the situation and, therefore, the Court 
has resolved that in order to curb the tendencies of strikes by lawyers following steps/ 
measures may be taken:— 
1. The Subordinate Courts shall not take cognizance of any resolution passed 
by the Bar Association to strike, and to stop judicial work. The District Judge 
concerned shall not entertain or circulate any such resolution amongst the Judicial Officers 
in his judgeship. The Judges shall sit in Court during Court hour and shall pass orders in 
the cases listed before them, whether the lawyers are present or not. 
2. The Judicial Officers must strictly adhere to Court hour. They shall perform 
the entire judicial work on the dais, and shall not accept any request to rise, or to stop 
judicial work on the request of lawyers or litigants. In case lawyers do not attend to 
work the judicial officers shall proceed to work in the following manner:— 
(A) Where the parties are willing they shall be heard personally and necessary 
orders shall be passed in case requiring no further evidence. 
168 

[27 February, 2006] RAJYASABHA 
(B) In matters fixed for evidence parties shall be allowed to file 
documents and do examinations/cross examinations of witnesses, if 
they so desire. 
(C) In all matters including suits, revisions, review, appeals (Civil and 
Criminal both), bails, urgent applications, etc. appropriate orders 
should be passed by the Judge even  in absence of lawyers. Such an 
order can also be an order dismissing the case for a default if legally 
permissible. 
(D) In criminal trials in the Court of Session or Magistrate the witnesses 
in attendance should be examined by the Public 
Prosecutor/Prosecuting Officer as the case be giving an option to the 
accused to either cross examine th e witnesses himself or bear the 
expenses for recalling of witnesses for cross examination on the 
date(s) next to be given. 
(E) The District Judges shall submit weekly report to the Court with 
regard to any incident, which may take place in the judgeship 
with compliance report of these directives. 
(F) In case any Lawyer or group of lawyers or litigants creates 
indiscipline in the court or try to intimidate the judge or lawyers 
or obstruct court proceedings, the Judicial Officer concerned 
should immediately inform th e District Judge, who shall 
immediately send for Police force and restore the functioning of 
the Court and initiate criminal proceedings against such lawyers. 
In case any damage is cost to the records or the court property, 
the District Judge shall immediately get a first information report 
of the incident lodged. 
(G) The District Judges shall arra nge for adequate police force to 
be kept in reserve in the judgeship, to be deployed for protection 
of the judicial officers, lawyers, litigants, court staff and the court 
property. If possible, video cameras should also be used. 
(H) The District Judge should inform the names of the persons involved 
in disrupting the court proceedings to the High Court forthwith so 
that appropriate proceedings for contempt of court can be taken. 
(I) The Judicial Officers shall not pe rform any judicial work in their 
chambers." 
(c) The Bar has not called off the strike so far.

The Anand Marriage Act, 1909 
820. SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH: W ill the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the An and Marriage Act for the Sikhs was 
enacted by Government in 1909; 
(b) whether the Act is still in operation as it has never been repealed; and 
(c) if so, whether Sikh marriages could still be registered under this Act? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND 
JUSTICE (SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Anand Marriage 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2006] 
Act, 1909 was enacted to remove doubts as to the validity of marriage 
ceremony common among Sikhs. The said Act does not lay down any 
substantive law with respect to registration of marriages. Sikhs are considered 
as Hindus under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 which provides for registration of 
a Hindu Marriage. Section 8 of Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 has empowered the 
State Governments to make rules relating to registration of marriages, and as 
such, State Government regulates the registration of Sikh marriages under the 
provisions of Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

834. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Small Scale Industries sector has requested Government to 
reduce the rate of interest and chalk out a revival package for the sector; and

grievances, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) Many small-scale industries (SSI) and their associations have been 
requesting from time to time, reduction in the rate of interest and a revival package 
for sick units. 
(b) Reduction of rate of interest and package for revival of sick units are 
within the powers of the banks. The Central Government, the Reserve Bank of India 
(RBI), and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) have accordingly taken the following 
initiatives in this regard: 
(i) The IBA has advised its member banks to lend to the SSI at interest rates 
within a band of 2 per cent above and below their respective prime 
lending rates (PLR). 
(ii) The Small Industries Develo pment Bank of India (SIDBI) has 
operationalised the Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) Fund under 
which loans are provided to the SSI at a rate of interest 2 per cent below 
the SIDBI's prevailing PLR. 
(iii) RBI had issued detailed guidelines to banks in January, 2002 on detection 
of sickness at an early stage and taking appropriate remedial measures and 
for rehabilitation of sick SSI units identified as potentially viable. 
(iv) Following the announcement of the Policy Package for stepping up credit to 
small and medium enterprises by the Central Government on 10th 
August, 2005 the RBI has issued detailed guidelines on 8th September, 2005 
relating to debt restructuring mechanism for facilitating restructuring of debt 
of all eligible SMEs, including SSIs. 
(v) The promotion and development of SSI is primarily the responsibility 
of State/Union Territory (UT) Administrations. The

in 12 states was conducted by the Institu te of Social Sciences, New Delhi in 
collaboration with the National Human Rights Commission. UNIFEM and 
the Ministry of Women and Child Development. The study was primarily on 
trafficking of women and children and not on prostitution/ child sex tourism.

(c) The study further confirms that women and children from less 
developed areas are trafficked to bigg er metropolis for commercial sexual

and socially discriminated especia lly those below the poverty line and 
belonging to SC/ST/OBC and other deprived sections of society are the 
most vulnerable. Girl children are extr emely vulnerable. It also says that 
qhances of trafficked victims contra cting diseases, es pecially HIV/AIDS 
etc., are very high. There is gross rights violations and the trafficked 
victims for commercial sexual exploitati on are subjected to lot of physical 
and mental torture. 
(d) In addition, to the existing overall constitutional and legal 
framework like IPC and ITPA which prohibit exploitation of women and 
children for commercial sexual exploitation, the Government has prepared 
a comprehensive national Plan of Action for Combating Trafficking of 
Women and Children 1998. The State Governments have been directed 
to take appropriate measures to im plement National Plan of Action. The 
Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956 is being amended to make it more 
effective. It also envisages constitution of Central Nodal Authority and 
State Nodal Authorities for Combating Trafficking of Women and Children. 
The Poverty Alleviation Schemes run by Government of India like National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme, Kishori Shakti Yojana and 
Swayamsidha etc. are some of th e schemes for economic and social 
empowerment. The Government also runs schemes of Short Stay Homes,

862.   MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Ho using and Land Rights Network, a 
human rights group, in its report has stated that there are about 10,000 
homeless women in Delhi and only 3 shelters are available for them; 
(b) whether the above group has demanded urgent measures to improve 
the lot of the shelter-le ss, especially women and children who are vulnerable 
to violence; and 
(c) if so, the action plan of Government to address this issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and 
(b) According to the information furnished by Housing and Land Rights 
Network, New Delhi, it has submitted a representation dated 19.1.2006 to the 
Government of NCT ot Delhi regarding the problem of homelessness in 
Deihi. According to the representation,  there are nearly one lakh homeless 
persons on any given day in Delhi, as per civil society estimates, of whom ten 
thousand are women. There are only 3 sh elters available to these homeless 
women, capable of accommodating rough ly 100 women. According to the 
representation, women and children tend to experience more acutely the 
adverse impacts of lack of adequate hous ing, such as increased risk of illness 
and starvation and heightened vulnerability to physical and sexual violence. 
The organization has called upon the Government of NCT of Delhi and the 
relevant municipal authorities to take various measures to properly address the 
situation, including its underlying causes. 
(c) The Government of NCT of Delhi has informed that the existing 
night shelters and shelters for des titute women are under occupied in 
comparison to their capacity. Effort s have been made to increase the 
occupancy. The Government of NCT of Delhi in partnership with reputed 
NGOs working for shelter less women is undertaking survey to assess the gap 
between demand and supply taking into consideration the capacity of all the 
existing women shelter

consistently low level of sex ratio are son preference, neglect of 
the girl child resulting in higher mortality at younger age, female 
infanticide, female foeticide, higher maternal mortality and male 
bias in enumeration of population. The last, but not the least, may 
be the latest trend of having preference for a small family of one

Need to restore faith in the system of delivery of justice in view of 
the recent judgement of a Session Court in the Jessica Lai 
murder case. 
SHRI SITARAM YECHURY (West Bengal): Thank you, Mr. Chairman, 
Sir, I want to raise a very important issue, which, in my opinion, 
219 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2006] 
concerns the entire construction of delivery of justice in our country. What has 
happened with the Jessica Lai murder case, and the entire media is full of 
reports of how tardy the investigations  have been, and how the complicity has 
been, and how the witnesses have turned hostile. Now, this is not a new thing. 
If this is what was to happen to page three celebrities, what is the fate of 
normal common citizens of our country? And this is a matter serious enough to 
draw the attention of the House so that we restore faith in the system of delivery 
of justice that we have in the Indian  people. We have seen in a series of 
cases, whether it has been the cases in Gujarat, whether it has been the cases 
of other VIPs that were involved—I do not want to take their names—whether it 
has been the cases that are continuously being reported in the media how 
witnesses are intimated, how the case is distorted and finally, the accused goes 
scot-free. So I think, something in this matter needs to be done, and the 
greater danger that I have with me is t hat Delhi, the National Capital, has a 
crime rate, which is 2.7 times higher than that of the national average. In 1998, 
there was 645 cases of murders of whom, only 376 cases were made out, and 
of whom conviction took place only in 160 cases. Out of 650 cases, convictions 
took place only in 160 cases. This is the sorry state of affairs. In this connection, 
since the Home Minister is also here, I would like to draw the attention of the 
House to the letter of the Chairman of the Law Commission of India, Justice 
Jagannath Rao, to Shri H.R. Bhardwaj, dated 13th August, 2004, and this letter is 
available on the website, from where I picked it up, where he says: "In recent 
times, it has become very common for witnesses in criminal cases to turn 
hostile on account of danger to their life and property or to that of their relations, 
consequent upon threats or intimidation by the accused..." It is in that context 
that the Law Commission had prepared this Consultation Paper. It goes on 
saying, "The Supreme Court in four recent judgements had dealt exhaustively with 
the subject of witness'anonymity and witness protection programmes. The 
Supreme Court has also stated that the Parliament must consider making a law 
on the subject at the earliest".

that are available on the Jessica Lai's  case are absolutely unacceptable. In 
any democratic civil society, if the system of delivery of

Government to seriously take note of this and immediately assure, through the

316 

[27 February, 2006] RAJYASABMA 
STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER 
         On the Civil Nuclear Energy Co-operation with the United States 
THE PRIME MINISTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I rise to 
inform this august House of the status of discussions with the United States on civil nuclear 
energy co-operation. Substantive aspects of this are reflected in the Joint Statement 
of July 18, 2006 that U.S. Presi dent Bush and I agreed upon during my visit to 
Washington DC last year. I would like to use this occasion to outline the context and 
core elements of the Joint Statement before detailing the status of the ongoing 
negotiations. 
Hon. Members are aware that our effort to reach an understanding with the 
Unitea States to enable civil nuclear energy co-operation was based on our need to 
overcome the growing energy deficit that confronts us. As India strives to raise its annual 
GDP growth rate from the present 7-8 per cent to over 10 per cent, the energy deficit will 
only worsen. This may not only retard growth, it could also impose an additional burden 
in terms of the increased cost of importing oil and natural gas, in a scenario of sharply 
rising hydrocarbon prices. While we have substantial reserves of coal, excessive 
dependence on coal-based energy has its own implications for our environment. 
Nuclear technology provides a plentiful and non-polluting source of power to meet our 
energy needs. However, to increase the share of nuclear power in our energy mix, we 
need to break out of the confines imposed by inadequate reserves of natural uranium, 
and by international embargos that have constrained our nuclear programme for over 
three decades. 
 Established through the vision of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru and  sustained by the 
commitment of scientists like Dr. Homi Bhabha, ournuclear programme is truly 
unique. Its uniqueness ties in the breadth of its overarching vision; of India mastering a 
three-stage nuclear programme using our vast thorium resources, and mastering more 
complex processes of the full nuclear fuel cycle. Consequently, our civilian and strategic 
programmes are deeply intertwined across the expanse of the nuclear fuel cycle. 
There are hardly any other countries in a similar situation. Over the years, the 
maturation of our nuclear programme, including the development of world-class thermal 
power reactors, has made it possible to contemplate some changes. These are worth 
considering if banefits 
317 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2 006] 
include gaining unhindered access to nuclear material, equipment, 
technology and fuel from international sources. 
However, international trade in nuclear material, equipment and 
technologies is largely determined by the Nuclear Suppliers' Group (NSG)—
an informal group of 45 countries. Members include the United States, Russia, 
France and the United Kingdom. India has  been kept out of this informal 
arrangement and therefore denied access to trade in nuclear materials, 
equipment and various kinds of technologies. 
It was with this perspective that we approached negotiations with the 
United States on enabling full civilian nuclear energy cooperation with India. 
The essence of what was agreed in Washington last July was a shared 
understanding of our growing energy needs. In recognition of our improved 
ties, the United States committed itself to a series of steps to enable bilateral and 
international co-operation in nuclear energy. These include adjusting domestic 
policies, and working with allies to adjust relevant international regimes. 
There was also a positive mention of possible fuel supply to the first two 
nuclear power reactors at Tarapur. US support was also indicated for India's 
inclusion as a full partner in the International Thermonuclear Experimental 
Research Project and the Generation IV International Forum. 
But more importantly, in the Joint Statement, the United States implicitly 
acknowledged the existence of our nuclear weapons programme. There was 
also public recognition that as a re sponsible State with advanced nuclear 
technologies, India should acquire the same benefits and advantages as other 
States which have advanced nuclear technology, such as the United States. 
The Joint Statement offered the possibility of decades-old restrictions being set 
aside to create space for India's emergence as a full member of a new nuclear 
world order. 
On our part, as hon'ble Members may recall from my suo motu 
statement on July 29 last year, we committed ourselves to separating the civilian 
and strategic programme. However, this was to be conditional upon, and 
reciprocal to, the United States fulfil ling its side of the understanding. I had 
stressed that reciprocity was the key and we expected that the steps to be 
taken by India would be conditional upon and contingent on action taken by the 
United States. I had emphasized then—and I reiterate today—that no part of 
this process would affect or compromise our strategic programme. 
318 

[27 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
I now come to the negotiations that have taken place in the past few 
months. While these have been principally with the US, there have been 
discussions with other countries like Russia, UK and France as well. At the 
political level, I have maintained contac t with President Chirac of France, 
President Putin of Russia, Prime Minister Blair of the UK. I have also raised 
this subject with the Heads of State/Government of Norway, Republic of Korea, 
Netherlands, Czech Republic and Ireland — all members of the NSG. I also met 
President Bush in New York last September and discussed implementation of 
the July 18th statement. In the same period, several American Congressional 
leaders and policymakers have visited India in the past few months, many of 
whom met me. We have amply clarified our objective in pursuing full civil 
nuclear energy cooperation for our energy security and to reassure them of India's 
impeccable non-proliferation credentials. 
At the official level, we have c onstituted two groups comprising key 
functionaries concerned with strategic and nuclear matters. They included the 
Department of Atomic Energy, the Ministry of External Affairs, the Armed 
Forces and my Office. These two groups were respectively m andated to draw 
up an acceptable separation plan, and to negotiate on this basis. The directive 
given to both groups was to ensure that our strategic nuclear programme is not 
compromised in any way, while striving to enlarge avenues for full civil nuclear 
energy cooperation with the international community. The negotiations by our 
officials have been extensive and prolonged, These have focused on four 
critical elements; the broad contours of a Separation Plan; the list of facilities being 
classified civilian; the nature of safeguards applied to facilities listed in the 
civilian domain; and the nature and scope of changes expected in US domestic 
laws and Nuclear Suppliers Group guidelines to enable full civilian nuclear energy 
cooperation with India. 
Hon'ble Members may be assured that in deciding the contours of a 
separation plan, we have taken into account our current and future strategic 
needs and programmes after careful deliberation of all relevant factors, 
consistent with our Nuclear Doctrine. We are among very few countries to 
adhere to the doctrine of 'No first Use'. Our doctrine envisions a credible minimum 
nuclear deterrent to inflict unacceptable damage on an adversary indulging in a 
nuclear first strike. The facilities for this, and the required level of comfort in 
terms of our strategic resilience have 
319 

RAJYASABHA [27 February, 2008] 
thus been our criterion in drawing up a separation plan. Ours is a sacred trust to protect 
succeeding generations from a nuclear threat and we shall uphold this trust. Hon. 
Members may, therefore, be assured that in preparing a Separation Plan, there has 
been no erosion of the integrity of our Nuclear Doctrine, either in terms of current or 
future capabilities. 
The Separation Plan that is being outlined is not only consistent with the 
imperatives of National security, it also protects our vital research and development 
interests. We have ensured that our three-stage nuclear programme will not be 
undermined or hindered by external interference. In fact, our three-stage programme will 
continue to receive the full support of Government including and through the construction 
of new facilities. We will offer to place under safeguards only those facilities that can be 
identified as civilian without damaging our deterrence potential or restricting our 
R&D effort, or in any way compromising our autonomy of developing our three stage 
nuclear programme. In this process, the Department of Atomic Energy has been 
involved at every stage, and the separation plan has been drawn up with their inputs. 
Therefore, our proposed Separation Plan entails identifying in phases, a 
number of our thermal nuclear reactors as civilian facilities to be placed under IAEA 
safeguards, amounting to roughly 65% of the total installed thermal nuclear power 
capacity, by the end of the separation plan period. A list of some other DAE facilties may 
be added to the list of facilities within the civilian domain. The Separation Plan will create a 
clearly defined civilian domain, where IAEA safeguards apply. On our part, we are 
committed not to divert any nuclear material intended for the civilian domain form 
designated civilian use or for export to third countries without safeguards. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, negotiations are currently at a delicate stage. In our dialogue 
with our interlocutors, we have judged every proposal made by the US side onmerits, but 
we remain firm in that the decision of what facilities may be identified as civilian will be 
made by India alone, and not by anyone else. 
At the same time, we are not understating the difficulties that exist in these 
negotiations. There are complex issues involved. Several aspects of the nuclear 
programme lend themselves in the public discussions to differing intepretation, 
such as the Fast Breeder 
320 

[27 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Programme or our fuel-cycle capabilities such as re-processing and 
enrichment requirements. The nature and range of strategic facilities that we 
consider necessarily outside safeguards constitute yet another example. We 
have however conveyed to our interlocutors that while discussing the 
Separation Plan, there are details of the nature and c ontent of our strategic 
requirements that we cannot share. We will not permit information of National 
security significance to be compromised in the process of negotiation. 
It is essential to recall that the July 18 Statement was not about our 
strategic programme; It was intended to be the means to expand our civilian 
nuclear energy capabilities and thereby to help pave the way for faster 
economic progress. In seeking to achieve this objective, we appreciate the 
need for patience to remove misperceptions that abound. I reiterate that India 
has an exemplary record on non-proliferation and this will continue to be so. All 
in all, one major achievement so far is that a change is now discernible in the 
international system. We believe that when implemented, the understandings 
reflected in the Joint Statement will give India its due place in the global nuclear 
order. The existence of our strategic programme is being acknowledged even 
while we are being invited to become a full partner in international civil nuclear 
energy cooperation. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, I must emphasize that the nation is justly proud of the 
tremendous work of our nuclear scientists and the Department of Atomic Energy 
in mastering all the key aspects of the full nuclear fuel cycle, often under difficult 
circumstances. The tremendous achievements of our scientists in mastering the 
complete nuclear fuel cycle — the product of their genius and perseverance — 
we not be frittered away. We will ensur e that no impediments are put in the 
way of our research and development ac tivities. We have made it clear that 
we cannot accept safeguards on our indigenous Fast Breeder Programme. Our 
scientists are confident that this te chnology will mature and that the 
programme will stabilize and become more robust through the creation of 
additional capability. This will create greater opportunities for international 
cooperation in this area as well. An important reason why the US and other 
countries with advanced nuclear technologies are engaging with India as a 
valued partner is precisely because of the high respect and admiration our 
scientists enjoy internationally, and the range and quality 
321 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2006] 
of the sophisticated nuclear progr amme they have managed to create under 
the most difficult odds. This gives us confidence to engage in these negotiations 
as an equal partner. 
As I said, many aspects of the proposed separation plan are currently 
under negotiation. It is true that certain assurances in the July 18 Statement 
remain to be fulfilled — the supply of impor ted fuel for Tarapur I and II, for one. 
Some elements, such as US support for India's participation in the ITER 
programme, have materialized. The issue of the nature of safeguards to be 
applied to facilites designated civilian also remains pending resolution. I seek 
the indulgence of this House not to divulge every single detail of the 
negotiations at this time. However, this august House can be assured that the 
limits are determined by our overarching commitment to national security and 
the related issue of the autonomy of our nuclear programme. Our Government 
will take no step that could circumscribe or cast a shadow over either. 
I am aware that concerns have been raised over information being shared 
with outsiders, but not with our own citizens. Members may be assured that 
nothing that could compromise our nucle ar deterrent has been shared with 
anyone. On this aspect there is no reason for concern or doubt. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, as I said at the outset, our approach is defined by the 
need to utilize the window of opportunity before us, to find a solution to our energy 
deficit. We have also been guided by the need to dismantle international 
restrictions, which, when achieved, co uld unleash our scientific talent and 
increase commercial potential in the nuclear and related sectors. The nation 
will be kept informed, through this august House. Thank you.
